stem: A 28-year-old athlete takes ibuprofen daily for knee pain and develops a gastric ulcer. Which of the following normally prevents the acidic gastric contents from digesting the stomach wall itself?

options.label: A
options.text: Neutralization of the luminal acid by secreted gastric lipase
options.misconception: An enzyme is being cast as an acid buffer.
options.explanation: Gastric lipase digests lipid; it does not neutralize acid. Neutralization at the wall is performed by bicarbonate secreted into the mucus layer.

options.label: B
options.text: A bicarbonate-rich mucus layer over tight-junctioned epithelium
options.misconception: None; mucus, bicarbonate, and tight junctions form the barrier.
options.explanation: The stomach wall is coated by bicarbonate-rich mucus that physically shields it and neutralizes acid, while tight junctions between epithelial cells block gastric juice from reaching deeper tissue.

options.label: C
options.text: Rapid emptying of the acid into the duodenum after meals
options.misconception: Reduced exposure time is being cast as the protective mechanism.
options.explanation: Chyme normally remains in the stomach for hours, so the wall needs a standing barrier; emptying speed does not protect the mucosa from acid.

options.label: D
options.text: Dilution of the gastric juice by large volumes of saliva
options.misconception: Dilution is being cast as meaningful protection against a pH of 1.5-3.5.
options.explanation: Saliva contributes little volume to the stomach and cannot meaningfully dilute its strongly acidic contents; the mucus-bicarbonate barrier is the protective layer.

options.label: E
options.text: Continuous inhibition of acid secretion by antral somatostatin
options.misconception: Suppressed secretion is being cast as the normal state of the stomach.
options.explanation: The healthy stomach secretes large amounts of acid with every meal; protection comes from the barrier at the wall, not from tonic suppression of secretion.

context: Learning objective: the gastric mucosal barrier. A thick bicarbonate-rich mucus coat physically shields the wall and neutralizes acid, and tight junctions between surface epithelial cells stop gastric juice penetrating deeper layers. NSAIDs weaken these defenses, producing ulceration.
imageCaption: Villi, SGLT1, mucosal barrier, pancreatic enzymes, micelles/chylomicrons, colonic water.
